questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Orthogonal Matrices
questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 \\ 4 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & -2 & -3\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ above. Which of the following statements are true?

- $A$ is a square matrix
- $A\cdot {A}^{T}=I$
- $A$ is an orthogonal matrix
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a square matrix $A$ is **orthogonal** if and only if

$$
A\cdot {A}^{T}={A}^{T}\cdot A=I
$$

where $I$ is the identity matrix.

With that in mind, let's examine the given statements. 

- Statement I is true. The number of rows in $A$ is the same as the number of columns. So, it's a square matrix.

- Statement II is false. Note that

$$
A\cdot {A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 \\ 4 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & -2 & -3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 4 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & -2 \\ -1 & 2 & -3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 21 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 14\end{aligned}]\ne I.
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $A\cdot {A}^{T}\ne I,$ our matrix is **not** orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

$$

questions.problem:
Solve for $x$ in $Ax=b$ given that the matrix $A$ is orthogonal, and 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5} \\ 0 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The inverse of an orthogonal matrix is equal to its transpose.

Hence, since $A$ is orthogonal, we have ${A}^{-1}={A}^{T}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}Ax & =b \\ {A}^{-1}Ax & ={A}^{-1}b \\ x & ={A}^{-1}b \\ x & ={A}^{T}b \\ x & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5} \\ 0 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ x & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Determinant of a Product of Matrices
questions.problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{\sqrt{17}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{17}} & \frac{4}{\sqrt{17}}\end{aligned}],\,Q=[\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{7} & \sqrt{5} \\ 4\sqrt{5} & 5\sqrt{7}\end{aligned}]
$$

Find $|\text{det}(PQ)|$ given that $P$ is an orthogonal matrix.
questions.worked_solution:
We use the following facts: 

- The determinant of a product is equal to the product of the determinants.

- The determinant of an orthogonal matrix $P$ is equal to $\pm 1.$

Applying these ideas, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\text{det}(PQ)| & =|\text{det}(P)\cdot \text{det}(Q)| \\  & =|(\pm 1)\cdot \text{det}(Q)| \\  & =|\pm 1|\cdot |\text{det}(Q)| \\  & =|\text{det}(Q)| \\  & =|2\sqrt{7}\cdot 5\sqrt{7}-\sqrt{5}\cdot 4\sqrt{5}| \\  & =50\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying True Statements About Orthogonal Matrices
questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the $n\times n$ orthogonal matrix $Q$ and the $n\times n$ matrix $P?$

- If $\lambda $ is a real eigenvalue of $Q,$ then $\lambda =\pm 1$
- If the determinant of $P$ is either $1$ or $-1,$ then $P$ is orthogonal
- $Q-I$ is singular
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $Q$ is orthogonal if and only if

$$
Q{Q}^{T}={Q}^{T}Q=I.
$$

To check that a matrix is orthogonal, it is sufficient to check that the above equation is satisfied.

Moreover, we have the following properties:

- For any orthogonal matrix $Q,$ we have ${Q}^{-1}={Q}^{T}.$

- $(AB)^{T}={B}^{T}{A}^{T}$ for conformable matrices $A$ and $B.$

With that in mind, let's inspect each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. If $\lambda $ is an eigenvalue of an orthogonal matrix $Q$ then $\lambda =\pm 1$

- Statement II is false. Every orthogonal matrix has the determinant equal to $\pm 1$, but not every matrix with the determinant equal to $\pm 1$ is orthogonal. As a counterexample, consider the following matrix:

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

The determinant of $P$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}det(P)=2\cdot 1-1\cdot 1=1,\end{aligned}
$$

 however, $P$ is not orthogonal since, for example, the first column is not normalized.

- Statement III is false. As a counterexample, consider the following orthogonal matrix:

$$
Q=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5} & -\frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5} & \frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}]
$$

We have that

$$
Q-I=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5} & -\frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5} & \frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{5} & -\frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5} & -\frac{2}{5}\end{aligned}]
$$

and $Q-I$ is not singular since, for example, it doesn't have proportional rows or columns.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

choices.value: None of the statements are true

questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the orthogonal matrix $Q?$

- $5Q$ is also orthogonal
- If $A=QB{Q}^{T}$ then $|det(A)|=|det(B)|$
- ${Q}^{3}$ is the zero matrix
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $Q$ is orthogonal if and only if

$$
Q{Q}^{T}={Q}^{T}Q=I.
$$

To check that a matrix is orthogonal, it is sufficient to check that the above equation is satisfied.

Moreover, we have the following properties:

- For any orthogonal matrix $Q,$ we have ${Q}^{-1}={Q}^{T}.$

- $(AB)^{T}={B}^{T}{A}^{T}$ for conformable matrices $A$ and $B.$

With that in mind, let's inspect each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. Computing the product $5Q\cdot 5{Q}^{T},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}5Q\cdot (5Q)^{T} & =5Q\cdot 5{Q}^{T} \\  & =25Q{Q}^{T} \\  & =25I \\  & \ne I.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Computing $|det(A)|,$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}|det(A)| & =|det(QB{Q}^{T})| \\  & =|det(Q)|\cdot |det(B)|\cdot |det({Q}^{T})| \\  & =1\cdot |det(B)|\cdot 1 \\  & =|det(B)|.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Let's consider the identity matrix

$$
Q=I=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

We have that $Q$ is an orthogonal matrix and also ${Q}^{3}=Q\ne O.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the orthogonal matrix $Q?$

- ${Q}^{T}$ is orthogonal
- The identity matrix $I$ is orthogonal
- $2Q$ is orthogonal
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $Q$ is orthogonal if and only if

$$
Q{Q}^{T}={Q}^{T}Q=I.
$$

To check that a matrix is orthogonal, it is sufficient to check that the above equation is satisfied.

Moreover, we have the following properties:

- For any orthogonal matrix $Q,$ we have ${Q}^{-1}={Q}^{T}.$

- $(AB)^{T}={B}^{T}{A}^{T}$ for conformable matrices $A$ and $B.$

With that in mind, let's inspect each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Computing the product ${Q}^{T}\cdot ({Q}^{T})^{T},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}^{T}\cdot ({Q}^{T})^{T} & ={Q}^{T}Q \\  & =I.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. The columns of the identity matrix are orthonormal. Therefore, $I$ is an orthogonal matrix.

- Statement III is false. Computing the product $2Q\cdot (2Q)^{T},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2Q\cdot (2Q)^{T} & =2Q\cdot 2{Q}^{T} \\  & =4Q{Q}^{T} \\  & =4I \\  & \ne I.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the orthogonal matrix $P?$

- ${P}^{T}$ is orthogonal
- ${P}^{-1}$ is **not** orthogonal
- $-P$ is orthogonal
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $Q$ is orthogonal if and only if

$$
Q{Q}^{T}={Q}^{T}Q=I.
$$

To check that a matrix is orthogonal, it is sufficient to check that the above equation is satisfied.

Moreover, we have the following properties:

- For any orthogonal matrix $Q,$ we have ${Q}^{-1}={Q}^{T}.$

- $(AB)^{T}={B}^{T}{A}^{T}$ for conformable matrices $A$ and $B.$

With that in mind, let's inspect each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Computing the product ${P}^{T}\cdot ({P}^{T})^{T},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{T}\cdot ({P}^{T})^{T} & ={P}^{T}\cdot P \\  & =I.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Computing the product ${P}^{-1}\cdot ({P}^{-1})^{T},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1}\cdot ({P}^{-1})^{T} & ={P}^{T}\cdot ({P}^{T})^{T} \\  & ={P}^{T}P \\  & =I.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Computing the product $(-P)\cdot (-P)^{T},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(-P)\cdot (-P)^{T} & =(-P)\cdot (-{P}^{T}) \\  & =P{P}^{T} \\  & =I.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

- Statement III is true. Since $A\cdot A^T = I,$ our matrix is orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

canonical_examples.problem: Find the inverse of the orthogonal matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069920/assets/0fdcc6a3e329666b00a45c05292d85ab2df6366ff38d5506233b6c15064d2149.png)

The inverse of an orthogonal matrix is equal to its transpose.

Therefore, since $D$ is orthogonal, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}^{-1} & ={D}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Determinant of a Product of Matrices
canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069920/assets/08c339defb7800dfbafef33db26281a6eb44740a61ff9d47bae8e9adc6af5f75.png)

Find $|\textrm{det}(PQ)|$ given that $P$ is an orthogonal matrix.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We use the following facts: 

- The determinant of a product is equal to the product of the determinants.

- The determinant of an orthogonal matrix $P$ is equal to $\pm1.$

Applying these ideas, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\text{det}(PQ)| & =|\text{det}(P)\cdot \text{det}(Q)| \\  & =|(\pm 1)\cdot \text{det}(Q)| \\  & =|\pm 1|\cdot |\text{det}(Q)| \\  & =|\text{det}(Q)| \\  & =|(-2\sqrt{3})\cdot 3\sqrt{3}-2\cdot 1| \\  & =|-18-2| \\  & =|-20| \\  & =20\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying True Statements About Orthogonal Matrices
canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the $n\times n$ orthogonal matrices $P$ and $Q?$

- $2Q$ is orthogonal

- $P^{-1}Q$ is orthogonal

- $PQ^T$ is orthogonal
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $Q$ is orthogonal if and only if

$$
Q Q^T = Q^T Q = I.
$$

To check that a matrix is orthogonal, it is sufficient to check that the above equation is satisfied.

Moreover, we have the following properties:

- For any orthogonal matrix $Q,$ we have $Q^{-1} = Q^T.$

- $(AB)^T = B^TA^T$ for conformable matrices $A$ and $B.$

With that in mind, let's inspect each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. Computing the product $2Q \cdot (2Q)^T,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2Q\cdot (2Q)^{T} & =2Q\cdot 2{Q}^{T} \\  & =4Q{Q}^{T} \\  & =4I \\  & \ne I.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Computing the product $(P^{-1}Q)\cdot (P^{-1}Q)^T,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}({P}^{-1}Q)\cdot ({P}^{-1}Q)^{T} & =({P}^{T}Q)\cdot ({P}^{T}Q)^{T} \\  & ={P}^{T}Q\cdot {Q}^{T}({P}^{T})^{T} \\  & ={P}^{T}(Q{Q}^{T})P \\  & ={P}^{T}(I)P \\  & ={P}^{T}P \\  & =I.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Computing the product $(PQ^T)\cdot(PQ^T)^T ,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(P{Q}^{T})\cdot (P{Q}^{T})^{T} & =P{Q}^{T}\cdot ({Q}^{T})^{T}{P}^{T} \\  & =P{Q}^{T}Q{P}^{T} \\  & =P({Q}^{T}Q){P}^{T} \\  & =P(I){P}^{T} \\  & =P{P}^{T} \\  & =I.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."
